newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cabinet threatens Duma, minister suspended.
newsitem.headline: Russian cabinet threatens Duma, minister suspended.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday he was disappointed with parliament's rejection of the cabinet's economic reforms, but added he would work further with the conservative legislature.

In the meantime another top minister brandished the threat of new parliamentary elections in a sign of growing irritation with uncooperative mood in the the communist-dominated State Duma lower house.

"It's a shame that the Duma did not back us," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying in reference to the Duma's refusal to back on Tuesday the the welfare reform and budget cuts which the government sees as crucial for economic reform.

"But we feel we have to look for solutions and...we will work to see these documents approved," he added speaking in the far easter city of Magadan where he made a brief stop on his way to the United States and China.

In a sharp contrast with the premier's conciliatory tone, Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev, who is in charge of the sensitive social sphere, warned that ministers' patience was wearing thin and raised the threat of dissolution.
Sysuyev told a news conference he personally did not favour new elections, acknowledging that the current make-up of the Duma was a fair reflection of voters' sentiment.
But he said the house was trying to force the government's hand and the executive could raise the issue of dissolution "in a tough manner".
"The Duma is doing all it can to create an extraordinarily tense situation by the autumn, to force the president to change policy. This will not happen," Sysuyev said.
"The situation will be even more difficult in autumn and the question of changing the Duma may be raised by the executive branch. It may raise it in a tough manner."

The chief architect of reform, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, on Tuesday accused the Duma of being "incapable of working" after it rose for its summer recess having rejected two out of three key pieces of economic reform legislation.
He stressed the question of whether to dissolve it was up to Yeltsin. The Duma's four-year term is due to end in December 1999, six months before Yeltsin's own final period in office.
The government is already pressing ahead with efforts to restore the public finances. It can rely on Yeltsin's powers to rule by decree, especially during the Duma's two-month recess.

Responding to a comment by the Duma's Communist speaker that parliament would not be rushed into decisions before the recess, Sysuyev said: "Only at a sprint can we solve our problems, and I don't know the meaning of the word 'holiday'."

Kremlin sources said talk of dissolution was partly intended to spoil legislators' holidays. Although opinion polls suggest new elections would not change the overall balance of power, they would pose risks for individual deputies and parties.
The talk is also seen a measure of irritation among ministers who face difficulties in meeting various pledges, such as paying off pension arrears by the end of this month.

The Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky, responding to outspoken criticism of the poor state of the armed forces from a senior pro-government deputy, told a news briefing on Wednesday defence reforms would be the priority after pensions.
On a matter of more immediate embarrassment to the government, Yeltsin finally acted to suspend Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov, who has been at the centre of a scandal for several days.
Monthly newspaper Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret) printed pictures it alleged were taken from a video showing him sharing a sauna with naked women in a gangland nightclub in 1995.
Kovalyov, a former Communist, has denied wrongdoing but had asked the president to suspend him while he clears his name. Yeltsin's decree said he was suspended pending an investigation.

The scandal is a novelty in post-Soviet Russia but public opinion scarcely appears to have registered it. Russian media have devoted far more space to speculation on how the pictures came to be made public than on Kovalyov's alleged behaviour.
